SRS11-P1-1.solved: Final para: "What she had undertaken was not to decide whether the letters should arrive. It was to wait until she was asked a second time", and para 3: "he had not asked again." The other four options are, verbatim, the three village theories (fondness=Mrs Prell, disorder=schoolmaster, sparing Ilse=sister) plus a habit she can in fact account for.
SRS11-P1-1.note: Well built: the distractors are the explanations the passage itself raises and then sets aside by putting all three holders of them outside the room.

SRS11-P1-2.solved: "In January she took it out again and put it in a tin that had once held boiled sweets, on the shelf above the stove." The stem's "eventually" is doing real work: C (drawer under the scales) is the intermediate resting place.
SRS11-P1-2.note: C is a genuine trap for a student who stops reading at the first sentence of the paragraph; the rest are inventions.

SRS11-P1-3.solved: "a strange, lawyerly way of speaking for a man she had never heard use a word of more than two syllables" — the clause is an explicit contrast between the register of the request and the man making it.
SRS11-P1-3.note: E ("he had written the words out beforehand and learned them") is the nearest miss and is a real reach away from exclusivity: a plain man producing lawyerly phrasing invites the thought that the words came from a lawyer. It is an added assumption, not a passage line, so C stands - but E is the one to watch if this item ever misbehaves in the field.

SRS11-P1-4.solved: Para 2 is three theories held by people who were not present; para 3 opens "None of the three had been in the sorting room on the morning Bryn Cadoc came in" and then narrates the scene from Ottilie's own memory ("she remembered thinking").
SRS11-P1-4.note: The contrast is signposted by the paragraph's first sentence, so this is easier than most organization items of this type.

SRS11-P1-5.solved: "Ottilie had had leisure to consider that the promise had been a foolish one" - thirty-one years of it. The sense is opportunity/ample time, not recreation.
SRS11-P1-5.note: B (ease of mind) is refuted by the content of what she considered; C and D are the primary-sense traps the item is built to catch.

SRS11-P2-1.solved: Para 2 gives the mechanism (a cast off a mould taken off another cast shrinks twice); para 3 finds sixty-one sitting "a further step down". That is the whole subject of the piece.
SRS11-P2-1.note: See the leakage note on SRS11-P2-3: that item's key is the same proposition stated from Bramm's side.

SRS11-P2-2.solved: "Every one of them had been bought between 1919 and 1923, and no cast bought in those five years fell into the other group."
SRS11-P2-2.note: A, B and D name attributes the passage never mentions at all - display rooms, handwriting, plaster colour - so the field narrows to two without reading. E is the only working distractor.

SRS11-P2-3.solved: Para 4: moulding shop flooded and "out of use for four years", the 1920 catalogue "the largest it ever issued", and "A workshop that is selling more heads than it can mould must be getting them from somewhere."
SRS11-P2-3.note: LEAKAGE: this key and the key to SRS11-P2-1 are one proposition seen from two ends. A student who has answered either has the other. See my cross-item report.

SRS11-P2-4.solved: "The complaint was minuted, thanked, and not acted upon" - the triplet is itself dry - plus "the only contemporary notice of a difference that anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers at any time in the seventy years that followed. Vass says so twice." The last three words are the tell: he is pressing the point.
SRS11-P2-4.note: HEDGE PRESENT, NOT KEY: A ("unwilling to say whether anybody was at fault") is the classic declines-to-adjudicate option and is wrong. B is directly refuted by "anyone could have measured with a pair of callipers". This is one of the four items in the batch that actively punishes the hedging heuristic.

SRS11-P2-5.solved: "they answer to one another closely but not to the rest" - the sixty-one match each other's measurements. Correspond to.
SRS11-P2-5.note: C (reply to) is the primary-sense trap; D (be responsible to) is the other live idiom ("answer to a superior") and is well chosen.

SRS11-P3-1.solved: Nineteen days forward over twenty-two years (para 1), of which eleven came after the walking frequency doubled (para 3), while the clearance is ruled out (para 4) and rising February temperature is conceded but declared unusable because "she cannot take her own boots out of it" (para 5). Multiple causes, none separable.
SRS11-P3-1.note: HEDGE PRESENT AND IS THE KEY - but I would not score it as a hedging tell. The passage's explicit conclusion is that the figure cannot be attributed, so the non-committal option is non-committal because the source is. A and B are contradicted outright; C and E are fabrications.

SRS11-P3-2.solved: "In 2004 she began walking the heath weekly instead of fortnightly."
SRS11-P3-2.note: D is refuted two sentences later ("The route did not change and the banks did not change"). A, B, C are unmentioned. Nearly a gift item.

SRS11-P3-3.solved: "If the opening of those banks to the sun were what was moving the dates, the two cleared banks should have run ahead of the other three from 1999 onward. They did not." A failed prediction rules the clearance out as the mover; it does not rule out its contributing with everything else, which is why the key needs "by itself".
SRS11-P3-3.note: A is the exact inversion of the stated finding - good. The qualifier "by itself" is the sort of soft hedge my tally counts on the loose reading; here it is doing genuine logical work rather than dodging.

SRS11-P3-4.solved: "What she disputes is the use that has been made of her figure. Nineteen days has now appeared twice in print as evidence of a warming climate... and she has written to both." Writing to both publications is the behavioural evidence of irritation.
SRS11-P3-4.note: HEDGE PRESENT, NOT KEY: A ("reluctance to say whether the figure means anything at all") is wrong - she is perfectly definite about what it cannot show. B is the nearest miss and a mild reach away from exclusivity: she says the record cannot be evidence of warming, not that it is worthless, and the distinction is fine enough that a careless strong student could take B. I still call this exclusive, but it is the second-thinnest margin in the batch.

SRS11-P3-5.solved: "A record of this kind... is only as sound as the walking behind it." The quality transferred from the walking to the record is trustworthiness, not good sense.
SRS11-P3-5.note: A (sensible) is the well-set trap - "a sound argument" is the commoner collocation - but it cannot pass through the "as X as the walking" construction, since walking is not sensible. B/C/E are the other live senses of the word and are correctly all wrong. One of the better vocabulary items here.

SRS11-P4-1.solved: Last paragraph, flat out: "He was right and I was wrong, and the argument took ten minutes, which was nine more than it should have." The whole piece is built to arrive there.
SRS11-P4-1.note: HEDGE PRESENT, NOT KEY: A ("uncertainty about what passed between them") is wrong - "I know what it looked like from where he was sitting, and I know what it was." C is refuted by "It was not modesty"; E by the fact that she refused the credit he offered. LEAKAGE: see SRS11-P4-4, which turns on the same two sentences.

SRS11-P4-2.solved: "He did not pay me in money. He paid me in books... I could have the duplicates from his own shelves instead."
SRS11-P4-2.note: D (thirty pounds in March) is a decent trap - the sum is in the passage, as what he had for the whole edition, not as what he paid her. A is refuted by the books themselves.

SRS11-P4-3.solved: "He had not asked me first. He said it as a thing already decided, which was the way he said most things."
SRS11-P4-3.note: A (making up for having paid her so little) is a plausible outside inference with no line behind it - the payment discussion is closed in para 2 and never linked to the title page. It is a reach, not a defensible second, but it is the option most likely to draw a thoughtful wrong answer. C is refuted by "He argued for about ten minutes".

SRS11-P4-4.solved: "It was not modesty. It was that I did not want to be found out later in a claim I could not defend" (the scruple renamed as self-protection) plus "the argument took ten minutes, which was nine more than it should have" (the impatience).
SRS11-P4-4.note: HEDGE PRESENT, NOT KEY: B ("still unsure whether the refusal was the right one") is refuted by "He was right and I was wrong." A is refuted by "It was not modesty." C is the sentimental option and is refuted by the impatience. LEAKAGE: this key and SRS11-P4-1's key are both read off the same closing two sentences; they are near-duplicates in what they test.

SRS11-P4-5.solved: "He was plain with me about it. He wrote that he had thirty pounds for the whole edition, that thirty pounds would not buy four hundred and eleven letters from anybody" - he stated an awkward financial fact directly. Candid.
SRS11-P4-5.note: The construction "plain WITH me" already forces the candid sense; a student who notices the preposition can answer without the sentence after it. Minor, but it is a small structural shortcut.

SRS11-P5-1.solved: Opening: "when the lettering on a village war memorial goes shallow, the parish should leave it shallow", and the close: "The wear is the one part of a memorial that cannot be commissioned."
SRS11-P5-1.note: C is a compromise/middle-way option (photograph, then re-cut) and is NOT the key - a second place where the batch declines to reward split-the-difference reading. B is the position the essay opens by naming as the fashionable one.

SRS11-P5-2.solved: By elimination, and uncomfortably. B, C and D are flatly contrary to the passage (nothing was moved, no name was omitted - "every name could still be read" - and the stone's failure to keep a letter is the reason for the work, not the writer's grievance). That leaves A, which at least has a line behind it: the roll was cut "a good deal deeper than the original", and depth is the one departure the writer flags in a sentence otherwise conceding fidelity ("in the same face, in the same places").
SRS11-P5-2.second_defensible: E - "the money could have been spent to better purpose". The essay ends "Chaldon paid eleven hundred pounds to have its only irreplaceable feature taken off", and para 4 says "money is easy to raise for a purpose nobody can be seen to object to". A student can read the eleven hundred pounds as the grievance. Against E: the writer never proposes an alternative use, and his complaint is that the spending did harm, not that it had an opportunity cost.
SRS11-P5-2.note: THE WEAKEST ITEM IN THE BATCH, and the one place I had to reach. The writer's actual objection is that re-cutting removed ninety years of wear - he would object identically had the letters been cut to the same depth, and he explicitly praises the mason. No option says that. The key I am forced to is a detail the essay reports but does not object to, and the stem's word "objection" is what breaks it. Either add an option naming the loss of the wear, or change the stem to "the writer notes that at Chaldon the lettering was". As it stands a strong reader is likelier to pick E than a weak one.

SRS11-P5-3.solved: "I will allow one exception and it is narrower than it sounds" - the concession - followed immediately by the narrowing: "not shallow, not faint in a raking light, but gone", "That is not a licence to re-cut the memorial. It is a licence to re-cut a name", and finally the removal of Chaldon from the exception altogether.
SRS11-P5-3.note: A describes para 4 (the tidy-people paragraph), which is a fair near-neighbour trap. The option's own shape is concede-then-qualify, which on a loose reading of "hedged option" makes this a case where a both-ways option IS the key - but here it is the key because it accurately describes what the paragraph does, not because it is non-committal.

SRS11-P5-4.solved: "I do not think the parishes that do this are careless of their memorials. They are the opposite. They are tidy people" (they mean well) set against the entire argument that the work destroys the memorial (they are wrong).
SRS11-P5-4.note: IMPORTANT FOR THE HEDGING TALLY - read this one carefully. Two options look non-committal and they behave oppositely. B ("unable to decide whether their reasons are good ones") is the true declines-to-adjudicate option and is WRONG. C is both-sides in content but fully adjudicates - it convicts them. If the author's hedge count scores C as a hedged key, I would push back: the option commits on both halves. E is refuted verbatim by "I do not think... careless", which is a gift.

SRS11-P5-5.solved: "But the memorial's office is not to be legible" - immediately after a paragraph about legibility, the sentence must mean the memorial's job/role. Proper function.
SRS11-P5-5.note: The hardest vocabulary item here and a good one: D is the primary modern sense, A and B are the two live archaic senses (the divine office; a kind office), E is the abstract-sounding decoy. All four are real senses of the word, which is what a vocabulary-in-context item should look like.

SRS11-P6-1.solved: Para 4: "A flagged floor sloped to a drain is what you would build for a dairy, and it is also what you would build for a retting and drying room for flax... I have been in the chamber a dozen times and I could not tell you which it was, and I know of nothing short of a new excavation that would."
SRS11-P6-1.note: HEDGE PRESENT AND IS THE KEY, but as with SRS11-P3-1 the passage itself refuses to settle, so the unsettled option is simply true rather than evasive. B is refuted (nothing came out of the floor in 1974); E is refuted (accounts begin 1851, after the flax). LEAKAGE: this key rules the Herron story out of court, which hands SRS11-P6-5.

SRS11-P6-2.solved: "It is flagged; the flags are laid to a fall of about an inch in seven feet; and at the low corner there is a drain."
SRS11-P6-2.note: "Flagged floor" also appears in the first sentence of the passage, so this is answerable from line one. All four distractors are unmentioned floor types - a student who has read anything can eliminate them. The easiest item in the set.

SRS11-P6-3.solved: "the jambs carry the sockets for a bar - on the passage side. A room barred from outside is a room for keeping things in. A family shutting themselves in would have wanted the bar on their own side." The observation exists to establish which side the room was shut from.
SRS11-P6-3.note: C, D and E are unsupported by any line (the jambs are called "original", which contradicts both C and D), so the field is really two wide. Also worth saying: the fuller purpose is to demolish the hiding-place tradition, and no option says that; B names only the intermediate step. It is still the only defensible answer, but the item under-asks its own paragraph.

SRS11-P6-4.solved: "the vault is bonded into the outer wall, course for course, and went up when the house went up."
SRS11-P6-4.note: Tagged inference, but the key is a near-paraphrase of an explicit sentence - this is a detail item wearing an inference label. A, C, D and E are each the negation of some part of that one sentence, which makes them clean but also makes the item mechanical.

SRS11-P6-5.solved: "The door is against it", "The window settles what is left of the story", and the sceptical framing of its pedigree: told "in that form for as long as anyone has been asking", into the 1888 county volume "without a question mark". He rejects it and treats its age as no recommendation.
SRS11-P6-5.note: THE BEST-DESIGNED ITEM IN THE BATCH for the hedging problem. D ("unwilling to say whether it is true") is a near-perfect trap, because the writer IS unwilling to adjudicate - about dairy versus flax, one paragraph later. A student who blurs the two questions, or who reaches for the hedge by reflex, takes D. The key is the flattest, most committed option on the page. Keep this item.
